definition: A program that reads the commands you type and runs them; on the lab server it is bash.
The window on your laptop where you type commands to a shell.
A secure way to log in to another computer over the network and run commands there.
A forwarded port that lets the browser on your laptop reach a program on the server (here JupyterLab) through your SSH connection.
A shared computer that many people log in to and run programs on at the same time.
Logging in with your password plus a one-time code from your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough.
A folder whose full history of changes is tracked by git.
A version-control program that records snapshots of your files so you can compare and undo changes.
One saved snapshot of changes in a git repository, with a short message that says what changed and why.
A named line of commits that lets you work on a change without disturbing the main line.
A GitHub page that proposes merging one branch into another, so someone can review the change first.
The original repository your copy came from; you pull tutorial updates from it.
Your own private GitHub repository that keeps the tutorial's history and holds your work.
The program behind a Jupyter notebook that runs your code cells; in this tutorial it is "SGTL (Python 3.12)".
A self-contained set of Python and packages with fixed versions, so results do not change when other software changes.
A package manager that installs Python and scientific libraries into separate environments.
A program that runs in your web browser and lets you write and run notebooks.
A file (.ipynb) that mixes code, results, figures and text in cells.
One stream of work inside a running program; more threads use more CPU cores at the same time.
One processing unit of a computer; all users of a shared server share a fixed number of them.
The fast working storage that a running program uses; when the server runs out, programs are killed.
Running a script so that it only prints what it would do, without changing anything.
A short written guess of a result, made before you run the code, so you can learn from the difference.
A test that runs your function on cases with known answers and prints PASS or FAIL without showing the solution.
The folder your shell is in right now; pwd prints it, and relative paths start from it.
Your own top folder on the server, written ~ in the shell; your files and the course software live under it.
The address of a file or folder; an absolute path starts at the top folder /, a relative path starts from the working directory.
A number that picks out one program listening for network connections on a computer; JupyterLab listens on one port, and the SSH tunnel forwards it to your laptop.
A named link from your repository to another copy of it, usually on GitHub, that git can push to and pull from; origin and upstream are the two remotes in this course.
Sending the commits you made on your computer to a remote, for example your private copy on GitHub.
Fetching new commits from a remote and merging them into the copy on your computer.
A plain-text table with one row per line and commas between the columns; the earthquake catalogs in this course are CSV files.
The | sign in the shell, which feeds the output of one command into the next command.
Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms: the fast library behind NumPy's matrix and vector arithmetic; it can start many threads unless it is told to use one.
A set of threads that a library starts once and reuses for parallel work; on the shared server each pool is capped at one thread.
The code of 40 letters and digits (often shortened to the first 7) that names one commit exactly.
A way to format plain text with a few marks, such as # for a heading and **bold** for bold text; notebook text cells and these docs use it.
Your record of AI help, one Markdown file per module in work/ai_log/ (for example work/ai_log/M01.md), with an entry every time AI help shaped your work.
A command that runs a program at a lower priority, so that it gives way to other people's work on the shared server.
A pandas table with named columns, like a spreadsheet inside Python.
A named block of code that takes inputs (arguments) and returns an output.
Doing a calculation on a whole array at once instead of looping over the items one by one.
A number that fixes a random-number generator, so the same "random" values come out every time.
The shortest distance between two points measured along the surface of the Earth.
The error report Python prints when a line fails; the last line names the error, and the lines above show where it happened.
A region that keeps one clock time, given as an offset from UTC (KST is UTC + 9 h); Python's zoneinfo module finds named zones such as 'Asia/Seoul' in a time-zone database.
Setting clocks one hour ahead for the summer months, so that in those months the clock's offset from UTC is one hour larger.
An invisible marker that some programs write at the very start of a UTF-8 text file; a program that does not expect it reads it as part of the first value.
A special floating-point value meaning 'not a number'; pandas uses it to mark a missing value.
An array of True and False values, one per element or row, that says where a condition holds.
NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes, for example one number with a whole array, without writing a loop.
The text in triple quotes just below a def line that says what a function does, what it takes and what it returns; help() prints it.
A Python string written with f before the opening quote, in which names in curly braces are replaced by their values.

korean: 나이브 시각, 시간대 정보가 없는 시각
definition: A date and time with no time zone attached, so Python cannot tell which instant on Earth it means.

korean: 인식 시각, 시간대 정보가 있는 시각
definition: A date and time with its time zone attached, so it names one exact instant.
The angle unit that NumPy's trigonometric functions use; a full circle is 2π radians, so 180° is π radians.
The angle at the Earth's center between the lines to two points on its surface.
One column of a pandas table: a list of values with a label (index) for each.
The row labels of a pandas DataFrame or Series; they stay attached to the rows when you select or sort them.
A rule that flattens the curved surface of the Earth onto a flat map.
In Matplotlib the figure is the whole image, and an axes is one plotting panel inside it with its own x and y axes.
A bar chart of how many values fall into each bin (interval), for example how many earthquakes have magnitudes in each 0.1-wide bin.
A plot with one marker per item at its x and y position, for example one dot per earthquake.
Writing labels and titles like a sentence: only the first word and proper names start with a capital letter, as in 'Depth (km)'.
A bar on a map that shows how long a given distance, such as 50 km, is on the map.
The longitude and latitude limits (west, east, south, north) of the area a map shows.
Latitude and longitude written as one decimal number, such as 35.85°, instead of degrees, minutes and seconds.
A plot of each earthquake's magnitude against its origin time, one marker per event.
A table of earthquakes with origin time, location, depth and magnitude, made by a seismological agency.
The earthquakes that occur in a region over a period of time.
The point inside the Earth where an earthquake rupture starts.
The point on the Earth's surface directly above the hypocenter.
The time when the earthquake rupture starts at the hypocenter.
The depth of the hypocenter below the surface, in kilometers.
A number on a logarithmic scale that measures the size of an earthquake; one unit means about ten times larger amplitudes.
A magnitude from the largest amplitudes on nearby seismometers, corrected for distance; the KMA catalog reports ML.
A magnitude computed from the seismic moment; unlike ML it does not saturate for large earthquakes.
Shear modulus times fault area times average slip, in newton-meters; the physical size of an earthquake.
Coordinated Universal Time, the reference clock used for all times in this tutorial.
Korea Standard Time, UTC plus 9 hours; the KMA catalog gives its times in KST.
The International Federation of Digital Seismograph Networks, which also defines standard web services for seismic data.
The U.S. Geological Survey's Comprehensive Catalog of earthquakes, which also lists larger Korean events.
The International Seismological Centre, which combines reports from many agencies into one global bulletin.
The Korea Open Government License that lets anyone reuse public data if they name the source.
The number of earthquakes in each magnitude bin, or at or above each magnitude.
The smallest magnitude above which a catalog records (almost) every earthquake in a region and period.
The rounding step of the magnitudes in a catalog, 0.1 for KMA ML; estimators must take it into account.
The rule that the number of earthquakes at or above magnitude M falls by about ten times per magnitude unit: log10 N = a - bM.
The slope of the Gutenberg-Richter law; it is close to 1 in most regions.
The productivity term of the Gutenberg-Richter law: log10 of the number of events at or above magnitude 0.
Choosing the model parameters that make the observed data most probable.
Events that happen at random times with a constant average rate, independently of each other.
The largest earthquake of a sequence.
An earthquake that comes before a larger earthquake nearby.
An earthquake that follows a larger earthquake nearby and belongs to its sequence.
A group of earthquakes that are close in space and time and are thought to be related.
A sequence without one clearly largest event, often lasting days to months.
The rule that the aftershock rate decays with time t after the mainshock as K/(t + c)^p.
Removing aftershocks and other dependent events so that the remaining events behave like independent background earthquakes.
Earthquakes that were not triggered by earlier earthquakes.
A distance in space, time and magnitude to the most likely parent event (Zaliapin and Ben-Zion), used to separate clusters from background.
The Epidemic-Type Aftershock Sequence model, in which every earthquake can trigger others and the rates add up.
A record of ground motion against time at one station.
An instrument that measures ground motion.
A site with a seismometer, named by a network code and a station code.
A two-letter code for the network a station belongs to, for example KS (KMA) or KG (KIGAM).
One recorded component of a station, named with three letters such as HHZ (band, instrument type, orientation).
The direction of motion a channel records: vertical (Z), north (N) or east (E).
The number of samples recorded per second, in hertz.
Half the sampling rate: the highest frequency a sampled signal can represent.
The raw integer numbers that a digitizer records, before the instrument response is removed.
How the instrument turns ground motion into recorded counts, as a function of frequency.
A compact way to write an instrument response as a ratio of two polynomials.
An XML file format for station locations, channels and instrument responses.
A standard binary file format for waveform data.
Seismogram Transfer Program: a client that fetches waveforms from a data center with your personal account.
Waveform data recorded all the time, as opposed to short windows cut around known events.
The displacement, velocity or acceleration of the ground at a station.
A filter that keeps the frequencies between two corner frequencies and removes the rest.
The amplitude of a signal at each frequency.
The direction from the earthquake to a station, measured clockwise from north.
The direction from a station back toward the earthquake, measured clockwise from north.
Horizontal components rotated to point along (R) and across (T) the direction from the source to the station.
A seismic wave that travels through the inside of the Earth: P or S.
A seismic wave that travels along the Earth's surface; it is slower than body waves and often largest at long distances.
The compressional body wave; it is the fastest wave and arrives first.
The shear body wave; it is slower than P and usually larger on the horizontal components.
The time a seismic phase reaches a station.
A measured arrival time of a seismic phase (P or S) at one station, made by a person or a program.
How much larger the signal is than the background noise.
The ratio of a short-term average to a long-term average of signal amplitude; a sudden rise marks a new arrival.
The moment a detector declares that a signal has started, for example when STA/LTA rises above a threshold.
Whether the first P-wave motion is up (compression) or down (dilatation).
A neural network trained on labeled seismograms to find P and S arrivals, such as PhaseNet.
Grouping picks from many stations into events, so that each pick belongs to one earthquake.
Finding earthquakes in continuous data.
Scanning continuous data with the waveforms of a known earthquake to find similar, often smaller, events.
A measure of how similar two signals are at each relative time shift.
The time a seismic wave takes to travel from the source to a station.
Seismic wave speeds as a function of depth; this tutorial uses layered one-dimensional models.
p = sin(i)/v, which stays constant along a ray in a layered Earth.
The angle between a ray leaving the source and the downward vertical.
The boundary between the crust and the mantle, about 30-35 km deep under South Korea.
A wave that travels along a layer boundary, such as Pn along the Moho; in this tutorial only a travel-time idea, never used for location.
A plot of S-P time against P arrival time; its slope is Vp/Vs minus 1, and the line reaches zero S-P time at the origin time.
The ratio of P-wave speed to S-wave speed; about 1.73 in many crustal rocks.
The delay between the S and P arrivals at a station; it grows with distance from the source.
Locating each earthquake on its own from its arrival times and a velocity model.
An observed value minus the value the model predicts, for example an arrival time.
A single number that measures how badly a model fits the data; location searches for its minimum.
Trying every point on a grid of candidate answers and keeping the best one.
Iterative linearized location: start from a guess, fit the time residuals with small changes, and repeat.
The matrix of partial derivatives of the predicted times with respect to the hypocenter coordinates and origin time.
Choosing the model that makes the sum of squared residuals smallest.
A matrix that describes the uncertainty of estimated parameters and how their errors trade off.
The region where the true epicenter probably lies, drawn from the covariance matrix.
The largest angle between neighboring stations as seen from the epicenter; a large gap means a poorly constrained location.
The root mean square of the travel-time residuals of one event.
A standard USGS program that locates earthquakes in layered velocity models.
The SGTL processing toolchain that runs picking, location, relocation and focal mechanisms in sequence.
Improving the locations of nearby events relative to each other by using differences of travel times.
The difference between the arrival times of the same phase from two events at one station.
The observed minus the predicted differential time of an event pair at one station.
The standard double-difference relocation program (Waldhauser 2001).
Cross-correlation choosing a lag one full period off, because two neighboring peaks look alike.
Adding a penalty that keeps model changes small so an inversion stays stable.
The ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value of a matrix; a large number means an unstable inversion.
Estimating uncertainty by repeating an analysis many times on resampled data.
A fracture in rock along which the two sides have slipped past each other.
The relative movement of the two sides of a fault during an earthquake.
The compass direction of a horizontal line on the fault plane, chosen so that the fault dips to the right.
The angle of the fault plane below the horizontal, from 0 to 90 degrees.
The direction of slip within the fault plane, measured from the strike direction.
A fault on which the two sides slide horizontally past each other (rake near 0 or 180 degrees).
A fault on which the upper side moves down; the crust is extended (rake near -90 degrees).
A fault on which the upper side moves up; the crust is shortened (rake near +90 degrees).
The orientation of the fault and the direction of slip, estimated from seismic waves.
An imaginary small sphere around the hypocenter on which the directions of rays leaving the source are plotted.
Drawing the rays that leave the source downward, as seen from above, on a flat circle.
A printed net for projecting directions on a sphere onto a flat circle by hand.
One of the two planes on which P-wave amplitude is zero; one of them is the fault plane.
The nodal plane that is not the fault plane.
The pressure (P) and tension (T) axes, which lie halfway between the two nodal planes.
The map-view drawing of a focal mechanism, with the compressional quadrants shaded.
How P-wave and S-wave amplitudes vary with direction from the source.
The ratio of S-wave to P-wave amplitude, which adds information to polarities when estimating mechanisms.
A Python program, successor of HASH, that finds focal mechanisms and their uncertainty from polarities and S/P ratios.
The smallest rotation that turns one double-couple mechanism into another; 0 degrees means identical.
A symmetric 3-by-3 matrix that describes the forces of an earthquake treated as a point source.
The moment tensor of slip on a flat fault: two opposite pairs of forces with no net force or torque.
Compensated linear vector dipole: a non-double-couple part of a moment tensor with no volume change.
The volume-change part of a moment tensor, as in an explosion or implosion.
A part of a sphere (Tape and Tape 2012) on which every moment-tensor source type has a place, from explosion to double couple.
Treating an earthquake as happening at one point, which is fine when the wavelengths are much longer than the rupture.
The time history of moment release at the source.
The part of the wavefield that decays as 1/r and dominates far from the source.
The decrease of amplitude with distance because the wave energy spreads over a larger area.
The seismogram that a unit impulse source would produce at a station; synthetics are sums of Green's functions weighted by moment-tensor elements.
A seismogram computed from a source and an Earth model instead of recorded.
A method that computes synthetic seismograms in a layered Earth by summing over wavenumbers; PyFK uses it.
Finding source parameters by fitting synthetic seismograms to recorded ones.
How much of the recorded signal the synthetics explain, in percent.
A small shift allowed between data and synthetics to absorb errors of the velocity model.
Two ways to add up residuals: absolute values (L1, less sensitive to outliers) or squares (L2).
The change in shear stress in the slip direction plus effective friction times the change in normal stress (unclamping positive); a positive value brings a fault closer to failure.
A symmetric 3-by-3 matrix that gives the force per area on any plane through a point.
The stress parallel to a plane, which tends to make the plane slip.
The stress perpendicular to a plane; in Coulomb calculations tension (unclamping) is positive.
The friction coefficient reduced to include pore-pressure changes, often written μ' = μ(1 - B).
The fraction of a change in mean stress that appears as a change in pore-fluid pressure.
The pressure of the fluid in the pores and cracks of rock.
The fault whose slip causes the stress change.
The fault on which the stress change is calculated.
Formulas for the displacement and strain caused by slip on a rectangular fault in an elastic half-space (Okada 1992).
A uniform elastic body that fills everything below a flat free surface.
A rock's resistance to shearing, about 30 GPa in the crust.
The ratio of sideways contraction to lengthwise extension when a material is stretched.
Small daily stress changes caused by the tides of the solid Earth and the oceans.
Checking whether a pattern could arise by chance, for example by randomly rotating the stress field or the aftershocks.
